--- title: "Federated OMOP analysis with dsOMOP" subtitle: "A hands-on tutorial — exploring real hospital data across three sites, without the data ever leaving them" format: html: df-print: kable execute: warning: false message: false error: true --- Download the R script (.R) Download the source (.Rmd) # Welcome In this tutorial you will analyse **real-world hospital data** that lives in **three different hospitals at once** — and you will do it **without ever seeing or downloading a single patient's record**. The pieces: - **OMOP CDM** is a standard *shape* for health data. Every hospital stores its patients, diagnoses, drugs and lab results in the same tables (`person`, `condition_occurrence`, `drug_exposure`, `measurement`, ...). Learn it once, use it anywhere. - **DataSHIELD** is the safety layer. You send *commands* to each hospital; the hospital runs them on its own data and returns **only aggregated, non-disclosive results**. Individual rows never travel. - **dsOMOP** is the bridge that lets DataSHIELD speak OMOP. ::: {.callout-important} ## The golden rule You never hold patient-level data on your laptop. Every result is checked by a **disclosure filter** on each server before it is returned. If a result would describe too few people, the server hides it. This explains much of what you'll see. ::: We work with **MIMIC** (an intensive-care database, ~100 patients here) throughout. The plan, step by step: 1. **Connect** to the three sites. 2. **Explore** — what tables, patients, conditions and measurements exist? 3. Learn the **recipe** — how to ask the servers to build an analysis table, growing from a one-line recipe to a richer one. 4. **Filter** at extraction (by condition, sex, age). 5. Fit a real **regression model** and read the result. --- # 1. Connecting to the federation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(DSI) library(DSOpal) library(dsBaseClient) library(dsOMOPClient) ``` ::: Describe the three servers and log in (same training login on each, asking for the **`omop`** profile), then attach the MIMIC database under the symbol `"omop"`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} builder <- DSI::newDSLoginBuilder() builder$append(server = "nairobi", url = "https://nairobi.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") builder$append(server = "douala", url = "https://douala.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") builder$append(server = "dakar", url = "https://dakar.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") conns <- DSI::datashield.login(logins = builder$build()) ds.omop.connect(resource = "omop_demo.mimic", symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} Forgetting `profile = "omop"` is the #1 beginner mistake — without it the `ds.omop.*` functions aren't available. If that happens, log out and rebuild the login with the profile set. ::: --- # 2. Reading the map: tables and columns dsOMOP reads each site's schema **separately** — a real federation could have different tables on different sites. Here the three sites are consistent, so one view represents the whole federation. These are the clinical (`CDM`) tables: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tabs <- ds.omop.tables(symbol = "omop", conns = conns)[[1]] tabs[tabs$schema_category == "CDM", c("table_name", "has_person_id")] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| |table_name |has_person_id | |:--------------------|:--------------------|:-------------| |1 |person |TRUE | |2 |observation_period |TRUE | |3 |visit_occurrence |TRUE | |4 |visit_detail |TRUE | |5 |condition_occurrence |TRUE | |6 |drug_exposure |TRUE | |7 |procedure_occurrence |TRUE | |8 |device_exposure |TRUE | |9 |measurement |TRUE | |10 |observation |TRUE | |11 |death |TRUE | |12 |note |TRUE | |13 |note_nlp |FALSE | |14 |specimen |TRUE | |15 |fact_relationship |FALSE | |18 |location |FALSE | |19 |care_site |FALSE | |20 |provider |FALSE | |21 |payer_plan_period |TRUE | |22 |cost |FALSE | |23 |condition_era |TRUE | |24 |drug_era |TRUE | |25 |dose_era |TRUE | |26 |cdm_source |FALSE | |27 |metadata |FALSE | |achilles_performance |achilles_performance |FALSE | |attribute_definition |attribute_definition |FALSE |
::: ::: The columns of a table are the same across the three sites, so one view is enough. The `measurement` table is where labs and vital signs live: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.columns("measurement", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)[[1]] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|column_name |cdm_datatype |db_datatype |concept_role |fk_domain |is_date |is_sensitive |is_blocked | |:-----------------------------|:------------|:---------------------------|:-----------------|:-------------------|:-------|:------------|:----------| |measurement_id |integer |bigint |non_concept | |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |person_id |integer |bigint |non_concept | |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |measurement_concept_id |integer |bigint |domain_concept |Measurement |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |measurement_date |date |date |non_concept | |TRUE |FALSE |FALSE | |measurement_datetime |datetime |timestamp without time zone |non_concept | |TRUE |FALSE |FALSE | |measurement_time |varchar(10) |text |non_concept | |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |measurement_type_concept_id |integer |bigint |type_concept |Type Concept |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |operator_concept_id |integer |bigint |attribute_concept |Meas Value Operator |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |value_as_number |float |numeric |non_concept | |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |value_as_concept_id |integer |bigint |attribute_concept |Meas Value |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |unit_concept_id |integer |bigint |attribute_concept |Unit |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |range_low |float |numeric |non_concept | |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |range_high |float |numeric |non_concept | |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |provider_id |integer |bigint |non_concept | |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |visit_occurrence_id |integer |bigint |non_concept | |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |visit_detail_id |integer |bigint |non_concept | |FALSE |FALSE |FALSE | |measurement_source_value |varchar(50) |text |non_concept | |FALSE |TRUE |TRUE | |measurement_source_concept_id |integer |bigint |source_concept |Measurement |FALSE |TRUE |TRUE | |unit_source_value |varchar(50) |text |non_concept | |FALSE |TRUE |TRUE | |value_source_value |varchar(50) |text |non_concept | |FALSE |TRUE |TRUE |
::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Where would you look for...? diagnoses → `condition_occurrence`; medications → `drug_exposure`; lab values / vital signs → `measurement`; social facts → `observation`; hospital/ICU stays → `visit_occurrence`. Every one has a `person_id` linking a patient's records. ::: --- # 3. Who are these patients? Gender lives in `person.gender_concept_id`. Rank its values, **pooled** across all three sites: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.concept.prevalence("person", concept_col = "gender_concept_id", scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| concept_id| n_persons|concept_name | |----------:|---------:|:------------| | 8507| 55|MALE | | 8532| 35|FEMALE |
::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Concepts translate themselves You got `MALE` / `FEMALE`, not codes like `8507` / `8532`. Any `*_concept_id` column is automatically translated to readable labels — **concept translation is on by default** everywhere in dsOMOP. ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## A real-world aside: de-identification Intensive-care data is de-identified by **shifting dates**. For this teaching dataset the dates were re-anchored so its records run through **2024**, but in real clinical data the calendar is often deliberately distorted while **ages and intervals are preserved**. The lesson: derive age from the data against a known reference year — never assume "this year" means "now". We do exactly that in Section 7. ::: --- # 4. Discovering what was recorded The most common diagnoses, **pooled** and ranked by distinct patients: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.concept.prevalence("condition_occurrence", metric = "persons", top_n = 10, scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| concept_id| n_persons|concept_name | |----------:|---------:|:----------------------| | 4145513| 85|ECG: sinus rhythm | | 4140598| 60|ECG: sinus tachycardia | | 433753| 55|Alcohol abuse | | 320128| 45|Essential hypertension | | 432867| 45|Hyperlipidemia |
::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## What you are (not) seeing Counts are **banded** (rounded) so you never read an exact size, and any condition affecting **too few patients to be safe is simply not listed** — it is dropped on the server, never shown as a flagged or blank row. Absence here means "rare or absent", and you cannot tell which: that is the disclosure filter protecting individuals. ::: Don't know a concept's code? **Search** for it (the result is the same across sites, so we read the pooled view; we keep the most useful columns): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hits <- ds.omop.concept.search("hyperlipidemia", domain = "Condition", limit = 5, symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled hits[, c("concept_id", "concept_name", "domain_id", "vocabulary_id")] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| concept_id|concept_name |domain_id |vocabulary_id | |----------:|:--------------|:---------|:-------------| | 432867|Hyperlipidemia |Condition |SNOMED |
::: ::: And **look up** codes you already have: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.concept.lookup(c(320128, 432867, 3027018), symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| concept_id|concept_name |domain_id |vocabulary_id |standard_concept | |----------:|:----------------------|:-----------|:-------------|:----------------| | 320128|Essential hypertension |Condition |SNOMED |S | | 432867|Hyperlipidemia |Condition |SNOMED |S | | 3027018|Heart rate |Measurement |LOINC |S |
::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Your turn Find the `concept_id` for a condition that interests you with `ds.omop.concept.search(..., domain = "Condition")`. ::: --- # 5. Numeric measurements: shape matters Measurements store a number in `value_as_number`. `ds.omop.column.stats()` returns a **disclosure-safe** summary — counts, mean, sd, and a 5th–95th-percentile band (never the true min/max, which could identify a patient). Start with **heart rate** (`concept_id = 3027018`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.column.stats("measurement", "value_as_number", concept_id = 3027018, scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $n_total #> [1] 19315 #> #> $mean #> [1] 95.73897 #> #> $sd #> [1] 19.25921 ``` ::: ::: A picture of the distribution. `ds.omop.value.histogram()` returns disclosure-safe **bins per site** (clipped to the 5th–95th percentile, with sparse bins dropped); we put them on a common grid and draw the federation-wide shape: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} draw_hist <- function(concept_id, nbins, xlab, main, col = "#4C72B0", digits = 0) { h <- ds.omop.value.histogram("measurement", value_col = "value_as_number", concept_id = concept_id, symbol = "omop", conns = conns) bins <- do.call(rbind, h$per_site) bins <- subset(bins, !is.na(count)) mid <- (bins$bin_start + bins$bin_end) / 2 br <- seq(min(mid), max(mid), length.out = nbins + 1) # common equal-width bins grp <- cut(mid, breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE) # re-bin each site onto them agg <- tapply(bins$count, grp, sum); agg[is.na(agg)] <- 0 ctr <- round((head(br, -1) + tail(br, -1)) / 2, digits) barplot(as.numeric(agg), names.arg = ctr, las = 2, col = col, border = NA, xlab = xlab, ylab = "records", main = main) } draw_hist(3027018, nbins = 7, xlab = "Heart rate (bpm)", main = "Heart rate across the federation") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dsomop_files/figure-html/hr-hist-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Heart rate is **roughly symmetric** — a single central peak, mean ≈ median. Now contrast it with a lab that is **not** symmetric, **serum creatinine** (`3016723`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.column.stats("measurement", "value_as_number", concept_id = 3016723, scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $n_total #> [1] 3880 #> #> $mean #> [1] 1.530898 #> #> $sd #> [1] 1.378811 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} draw_hist(3016723, nbins = 9, xlab = "Creatinine (mg/dL)", main = "Serum creatinine across the federation", col = "#C44E52", digits = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dsomop_files/figure-html/creat-hist-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Symmetric vs skewed — why it matters Heart rate's mean sits in the middle of the bulk. Creatinine's distribution has a **long right tail** (a minority of patients with kidney injury), which **pulls the mean above the median** — so for creatinine the mean overstates the "typical" patient. Always look at the shape before trusting a mean; skewed labs are often summarised with the median, or modelled on the log scale. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Always check the units, too Not every measurement is clean. Body temperature (`3020891`) in this extract mixes **Celsius and Fahrenheit** records, so its histogram is bimodal and its mean (~88) is meaningless. A real federated project spends much of its time on this kind of **data-quality / unit-harmonisation** check before any analysis. ::: --- # 6. A categorical measurement: heart rhythm Some measurements store a *category* in `value_as_concept_id` instead of a number. Heart **rhythm** (`3022318`) is the classic example. Ask for a **pooled** federation-wide count with `scope = "pooled"`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.omop.value.counts("measurement", "value_as_concept_id", concept_id = 3022318, scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| n|concept_name |value | |----:|:-------------------|:--------| | 6530|Sinus rhythm |45877096 | | 2400|Atrial fibrillation |45883018 | | 2300|Sinus tachycardia |45879290 | | 665|concept_0 |0 | | 385|Sinus bradycardia |21499419 |
::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Two kinds of measurement A **numeric** measurement (heart rate *value*) → summarise with mean / sd / histogram. A **categorical** one (heart *rhythm*) → count each level. The coded values came back as readable labels (`Sinus rhythm`, `Atrial fibrillation`, ...); the `concept_0` bucket is the **unmapped** records. Any level too rare to clear the privacy threshold is simply **absent** — never a flagged row. ::: --- # 7. The recipe: building analysis tables Single aggregates are great for exploring, but to **model** anything we need a table with **one row per patient** and **one column per variable**. In dsOMOP you describe that table with a **recipe**, and the servers build it for you — still without sending any rows. A recipe has four elements: | Element | What it is | |---|---| | **variables** | the columns you want — each an `omop_variable(...)`: a `person` column, or something built from a `concept_id` in an event table | | **format** | *how* each variable is summarised per patient: `"sex_mf"`, `"binary"` (0/1 presence), `"count"` (how many records), `"mean"`, `"sd"`, ... (and `omop_variable_age()` builds age) | | **filters** | optional restrictions applied **during** extraction (Section 8) | | **output** | `omop_output(name, type = "wide")` — `"wide"` = one row per patient, exactly what a model needs | ## 7.1 Start simple The smallest useful recipe: just **sex** and **age**. Preview it (a server-side dry run that builds nothing), then execute it into a server-side symbol `M0`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec0 <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2024) ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide") ) recipe_execute(rec0, out = c(study = "M0"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: **Always inspect what the server built** — confirm the table exists, with the columns and the number of rows you expected: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.colnames("M0", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $nairobi #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" #> #> $douala #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" #> #> $dakar #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.dim("M0", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $`dimensions of M0 in nairobi` #> [1] 35 3 #> #> $`dimensions of M0 in douala` #> [1] 25 3 #> #> $`dimensions of M0 in dakar` #> [1] 40 3 #> #> $`dimensions of M0 in combined studies` #> [1] 100 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Why `year = 2024`? Age needs a reference year. This MIMIC extract runs through **2024**, so we anchor age there rather than to `today` — otherwise every rebuild of this page would silently age the patients. For your own data, set `year =` to its collection year (or use `reference = "index"` for age at cohort entry). The age **filter** in Section 8 takes the same `year =` so the two always agree. ::: ## 7.2 Grow it: numbers, flags and counts Now mix the variable *types* we met while exploring — a categorical (`sex`), a numeric mean (`heart_rate`), two **binary** condition flags (`hypertension` 320128, `hyperlipidemia` 432867), and a **count** (`n_visits`, how many hospital visits each patient has): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2024), omop_variable(table = "measurement", concept_id = 3027018, format = "mean", name = "heart_rate"), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 320128, format = "binary", name = "hypertension"), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 432867, format = "binary", name = "hyperlipidemia"), omop_variable(table = "visit_occurrence", format = "count", name = "n_visits") ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide") ) recipe_execute(rec, out = c(study = "M"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ds.colnames("M", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $nairobi #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" "hyperlipidemia" #> [5] "n_visits" "sex" "age" #> #> $douala #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" "hyperlipidemia" #> [5] "n_visits" "sex" "age" #> #> $dakar #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" "hyperlipidemia" #> [5] "n_visits" "sex" "age" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.dim("M", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $`dimensions of M in nairobi` #> [1] 35 7 #> #> $`dimensions of M in douala` #> [1] 25 7 #> #> $`dimensions of M in dakar` #> [1] 40 7 #> #> $`dimensions of M in combined studies` #> [1] 100 7 ``` ::: ::: **Inspect every variable in its natural way.** A numeric summary for the continuous columns: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.summary("M$heart_rate", datasources = conns)[[1]][["quantiles & mean"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 5% 10% 25% 50% 75% 90% 95% Mean #> 68.85334 70.28388 78.92535 88.44355 98.68583 104.52308 107.79092 88.63992 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.summary("M$n_visits", datasources = conns)[[1]][["quantiles & mean"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> 5% 10% 25% 50% 75% 90% 95% Mean #> 1.00000 1.00000 1.50000 3.00000 8.50000 29.80000 39.20000 10.54286 ``` ::: ::: A frequency table for the categorical / binary columns: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(ds.table("M$sex", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Data in all studies were valid #> #> Study 1 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 2 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 3 : No errors reported from this study ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | ds.table("M$sex", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]| |:--|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------:| |F | 43| |M | 57| |NA | 0|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(ds.table("M$hypertension", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Data in all studies were valid #> #> Study 1 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 2 : No errors reported from this study #> Study 3 : No errors reported from this study ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | ds.table("M$hypertension", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]| |:--|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------:| |0 | 47| |1 | 53| |NA | 0|
::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## `binary` vs `count` `format = "binary"` answers *"does this patient have the condition at all?"* (0/1) — perfect for a yes/no risk factor. `format = "count"` answers *"how many records?"* — here, how many visits. Notice `n_visits` is **right-skewed**: most patients have a few visits, a handful have many. ::: ## 7.3 One recipe, several tables: multiple outputs A recipe can declare **more than one output**, each selecting a **different subset of the variables** — so a single extraction can produce several purpose-built tables at once (e.g. a demographics table and a clinical table) instead of re-running the extraction. List them with `outputs = list(...)` and map each name to its own symbol: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_multi <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2024), omop_variable(table = "measurement", concept_id = 3027018, format = "mean", name = "heart_rate"), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 320128, format = "binary", name = "hypertension") ), outputs = list( omop_output(name = "demographics", variables = c("sex", "age"), type = "wide"), omop_output(name = "clinical", variables = c("heart_rate", "hypertension"), type = "wide") ) ) recipe_execute(rec_multi, out = c(demographics = "DEMO", clinical = "CLIN"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: Ratify that **both** tables were built, each with only its own columns (plus the `person_id` key that lets you join them later): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.colnames("DEMO", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $nairobi #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" #> #> $douala #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" #> #> $dakar #> [1] "person_id" "sex" "age" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.colnames("CLIN", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> $nairobi #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" #> #> $douala #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" #> #> $dakar #> [1] "person_id" "heart_rate" "hypertension" ``` ::: ::: --- # 8. Filtering at extraction Often you only want a **subpopulation**. The cleanest way is to filter **while extracting** — add a `filters` element so the servers only ever build the rows you asked for. Filters can only ever **shrink** a population (the per-patient disclosure gate still runs on the result), so they are safe. Here we combine three filters — keep only **females**, **aged 65+**, who **have hypertension**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_sub <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2024), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 432867, format = "binary", name = "hyperlipidemia") ), filters = list( female = omop_filter_sex("F"), elderly = omop_filter_age(min = 65, year = 2024), with_htn = omop_filter_has_concept(concept_id = 320128, table = "condition_occurrence") ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide") ) recipe_execute(rec_sub, out = c(study = "SUB"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` #> Error: #> ! There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors() ``` ::: ::: **Check the filters did what you meant** — the cohort is smaller, everyone is female, and the minimum age respects the 65+ filter: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ds.dim("SUB", datasources = conns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` #> Error: #> ! There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors() ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(ds.table("SUB$sex", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` #> Error: #> ! There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors() ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ds.summary("SUB$age", datasources = conns)[[1]][["quantiles & mean"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` #> Error: #> ! There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} These filters are just a demonstration — we built `SUB` to show how filtering narrows a cohort, but we go back to the full table `M` for the model below. The safe filter types are the ones that can only shrink a population: `omop_filter_sex()`, `omop_filter_age()` / age groups, `omop_filter_has_concept()`, and ranges; an over-narrow filter (e.g. a single birth year) is rejected so it cannot fingerprint a person. ::: --- # 9. A real model: what predicts a diagnosis? We have the person-level table `M`. Let's start with a clean question: **does hyperlipidemia become more likely with age, and does sex matter?** A logistic regression (`family = "binomial"`), fitted jointly across the three hospitals: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit1 <- ds.glm( formula = "M$hyperlipidemia ~ M$age + M$sex", family = "binomial", datasources = conns) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} or_table <- function(fit) { co <- fit$coefficients data.frame( term = rownames(co), OR = round(co[, "P_OR"], 3), CI_low = round(co[, "low0.95CI.P_OR"], 3), CI_high = round(co[, "high0.95CI.P_OR"], 3), p_value = signif(co[, "p-value"], 3), row.names = NULL ) } or_table(fit1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | OR| CI_low| CI_high| p_value| |:-----------|-----:|------:|-------:|--------:| |(Intercept) | 0.010| 0.001| 0.089| 7.24e-05| |M$age | 1.073| 1.037| 1.109| 4.43e-05| |M$sexM | 0.986| 0.402| 2.418| 9.75e-01|
::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Reading the result (`OR` = odds ratio) - **age** is a clear, **significant** predictor — the odds of hyperlipidemia rise a few percent per year of age (OR > 1, p well below 0.05, confidence interval entirely above 1). - **sex** is **not** significant here (OR ≈ 1, p ≈ 1, CI straddling 1). That is exactly how you read a `ds.glm` table: one clear effect, one null — produced without ever touching a patient record. ::: Now a **multivariable** model: does hypertension depend on age and sex **after adjusting for** hyperlipidemia? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit2 <- ds.glm( formula = "M$hypertension ~ M$age + M$sex + M$hyperlipidemia", family = "binomial", datasources = conns) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} or_table(fit2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | OR| CI_low| CI_high| p_value| |:----------------|-----:|------:|-------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 0.084| 0.013| 0.384| 0.01450| |M$age | 1.047| 1.014| 1.081| 0.00495| |M$sexM | 0.419| 0.173| 1.014| 0.05360| |M$hyperlipidemia | 1.335| 0.527| 3.382| 0.54200|
::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Adjustment, and the limits of a small sample Age stays a significant predictor of hypertension; sex is **borderline**; and the hyperlipidemia adjustment is not significant. On a **~100-patient** demo, power is limited — "estimable and converged" is the success criterion here, not a definitive clinical claim. The companion GiBleed study (next) has ~2,700 patients and delivers a strongly significant result. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} DSI::datashield.logout(conns) ``` ::: --- # Where to go next You now have the full toolkit: **connect → explore (conditions, numeric shape, categorical levels) → recipe (variables / format / filters / output, single or multiple) → preview → execute → ratify → summarise → model**, all under a disclosure filter that kept every patient private. ::: {.callout-note} ## Coming next The **[exercise sheet](omop-exercises.qmd)** lets you practise everything here on new variables and a new model (with hints and a worked solution). Then a second vignette takes these exact tools to the larger **GiBleed** dataset (~2,700 patients) — where, with no numeric values to lean on, everything is treated as **boolean presence** — for a more powerful study. :::
